If it isn't, removing the ground pin (properly) would not cause this. The ground pin only provides a path for electricity in the case something in the electrical device shorts out against the frame or case. The intent is the case/frame is attached to the ground so a short will follow the ground path via the ground pin (and blow the circuit fuse) instead of flowing through whoever is touching the device. Double insulated devices don't need the ground pin because the double insulation protects the user from shock.

That cord fried because there was a short (or simply a high load) somewhere which drew more power than the cord was rated to provide. If the short (or high load) was across the live and neutral, a ground pin (disabled or not) would offer no protection. You simply overloaded the cord. One could argue removing the ground pin would reduce the chance of this happening as it would remove one possible (high current) short path.

Assuming this isn't staged I could see one of two causes for this. 1) In removing the ground pin (bending it back and forth) she managed to cause a short (or partial short) in the adapter itself or 2) The reason she was removing the pin in the first place is she wanted to plug a very high load device with a ground pin into a cheap extension cord that didn't have the ground line.
